sections.Disease management: CV, infection, neurology, respiratory, renal, GI, and other systemic disease (haem/endocrine/toxicology/obstetric).
sections.Organ support & intervention: Medical treatment, organ support, and perioperative care.
sections.Practical procedures: Respiratory, cardiovascular, CNS, and other procedural knowledge.
sections.General patient care: Resuscitation, comfort and recovery, patient safety, and end-of-life care.

questions.question: A 77-year-old man is in the ICU after surgery for bowel perforation, with a background of hypertension and ischaemic stroke with full neurological recovery. On postoperative day 3 his blood pressure suddenly drops to 60/45 mmHg, and the ECG is compatible with atrial fibrillation. What is your first treatment in this specific case?
options: Prevention of embolic complications
Treatment of the underlying cause
Heart rate control
Electrical cardioversion
Chemical cardioversion
questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation is common in postoperative ICU patients, and all the listed measures are eventually appropriate, but a haemodynamically unstable patient must first be stabilised with electrical cardioversion. Rate control and treating the underlying cause are important but are not the immediate priority when the patient is hypotensive.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman was admitted to Intensive Care Unit (ICU) with no prior history of cardiovascular disease who underwent open surgical repair of an abdominal aortic aneurism 48 h earlier. An increase in high-sensitivity troponin from 110 to 220 ng/L (ULN <14 ng/L) was observed within 24 h of surgery. The patient did not have chest pain but is receiving morphine. The ECG is normal. Her haemoglobin level is 8.5 g/dL. Echocardiography shows normal left ventricular (LV) function in the absence of regional wall motion abnormalities. Which statements are applicable to this scenario

statements.label: A
statements.text: Teamwork discussion with the surgeon is needed to assess the risks and benefits of early therapy in this patient

statements.label: B
statements.text: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy can be included among the differential diagnoses

statements.label: C
statements.text: This patient suffered a perioperative myocardial infarction (MI) type 2

statements.label: D
statements.text: Additional information regarding the intraoperative course (e.g. hypotension, major bleeding, arrhythmias) is necessary to differentiate Type 1 MI from Type 2 MI

questions.explanation: ALL statements are true. Type 2 MI: rising troponin post-major vascular surgery + anaemia (Hb 8.5) + normal echo = O2 supply-demand mismatch without coronary thrombosis. Takotsubo is a differential (physical stress trigger) but echo shows normal LV function — Takotsubo typically shows apical akinesia. Intraoperative details (hypotension, bleeding, arrhythmias) are needed to confirm Type 2 vs Type 1. Multidisciplinary teamwork (intensivist + surgeon + cardiologist) is essential to weigh risks of antiplatelet/anticoagulation vs. surgical bleeding in the early post-op period.

questions.question: Concerning AKI after major surgery the following statements are true:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Approximately 40% of patients develop at least stage 1 AKI after major surgery

statements.label: B
statements.text: Urine output is more reliable for diagnosing AKI after surgery compared to serum creatinine

statements.label: C
statements.text: The definition of stage 1 AKI is different after major surgery because of the dilutional effects of administered fluids affecting the serum creatinine.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Major surgery is a risk factor for AKI

questions.explanation: Major surgery is a risk factor for AKI. A recent prospective study in 30 countries in more than 10,000 patients undergoing major surgery showed that approximately one in five (20%) of patients developed AKI after major surgery. The diagnosis of AKI immediately after surgery can be problematic because of dilutional effects of fluids on serum creatinine and physiological changes in urine output caused by increased ADH secretion after surgery, but definitions for AKI have not been changed to accommodate this. There is no evidence that urine output measurements are better than serum creatinine measurements at diagnosing AKI in this group of patients.

questions.question: The major indication for performing a cricothyroidotomy is:
options: Physician has no anaesthetic experience
Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate scenario
Major facial trauma
Two or more different methods of intubation have proven unsuccessful
Previous anaphylaxis to suxamethonium
questions.explanation: National guidelines establish that cricothyroidotomy should be performed in a 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' scenario, after failed attempts at intubation and oxygenation using a face mask and a supraglottic device. If two or more intubation attempts have failed but oxygenation is maintained, it is generally sensible to wait for assistance rather than proceed directly to a surgical airway.

questions.question: Concerning the technique of percutaneous tracheostomy:

statements.label: A
statements.text: The balloon dilation technique is contraindicated in a patient with an unstable cervical spine

statements.label: B
statements.text: The Grigg's technique uses a single tapered dilation technique

statements.label: C
statements.text: Use of local anaesthetic pre-procedure will obscure the anatomy and should be avoided

statements.label: D
statements.text: A chest x-ray must be requested post-procedure

questions.explanation: The Grigg's technique uses specialised (Howard Kelly) forceps to dilate the trachea over the guidewire, not a single tapered dilator - that describes the Ciaglia Single-Step technique. There is no absolute contraindication to percutaneous tracheostomy, and unless clinically indicated, routine post-procedure chest x-ray is unnecessary. Local anaesthetic infiltration is standard practice and does not meaningfully obscure surgical landmarks.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication or significant limitation to intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) insertion?
options: Moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation
Severe peripheral vascular disease with absent femoral pulses bilaterally
Cardiogenic shock refractory to inotropes and vasopressors
Rapid atrial fibrillation (ventricular rate 140–160 bpm)
Known aortic dissection involving the descending thoracic aorta
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic shock refractory to medical therapy is an INDICATION for IABP, not a contraindication. Moderate-to-severe AR is a contraindication (diastolic inflation worsens regurgitation). Severe PVD risks limb ischaemia. Rapid AF significantly reduces IABP efficacy as insufficient diastolic time is available for augmentation — while not an absolute contraindication, it substantially limits benefit. Aortic dissection involving the descending aorta is an anatomical contraindication.

questions.question: A temporary transvenous pacing wire is inserted via the right internal jugular vein for complete heart block. Pacing spikes with capture are seen on the monitor. The post-procedure chest radiograph is shown. Together with threshold testing and a 12-lead ECG, what does this radiograph appearance help confirm?
options: That the lead tip has perforated the right ventricular free wall
That the lead tip is appropriately positioned in the right ventricular apex
That the lead has looped back into the superior vena cava
That the lead tip lies in the right atrium, insufficient for reliable ventricular capture
That the lead is malpositioned within the coronary sinus
questions.explanation: Confirming correct position of a ventricular pacing wire requires threshold measurement, stability, a chest radiograph, and a 12-lead ECG together — the PACT module specifically lists all four. This radiograph is captioned as showing correct position of the ventricular pacing wire, consistent with the lead tip lying appropriately in the right ventricular apex. Perforation, coronary sinus malposition, atrial-only positioning, and SVC looping are all recognised malposition patterns, but are not what this particular radiograph demonstrates — and effective ventricular capture with a paced rhythm on the monitor is already inconsistent with a purely atrial or non-ventricular lead position.

questions.section: TBI Part III: Assessment and Management
questions.question: Which ICP monitoring device uniquely provides the dual advantage of measuring ICP continuously AND actively treating intracranial hypertension?
options: Ventricular catheter (EVD)
Intraparenchymal Camino fibre-optic probe
Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) sensor
Epidural piezoelectric ICP sensor
Subdural bolt pressure transducer
questions.explanation: A ventricular catheter (EVD) uniquely allows simultaneous continuous ICP measurement AND therapeutic CSF drainage to actively reduce ICP. Intraparenchymal probes measure ICP accurately but cannot drain CSF. Subdural and epidural recordings are unreliable and not recommended. EVD is especially valuable when hydrocephalus contributes to ICP elevation.

questions.question: A patient with severe ARDS is established on veno-venous ECMO via femoral-jugular cannulation. Blood gas sampling shows: pre-oxygenator (pre-membrane) PO2 31 mmHg, SO2 60%; post-oxygenator (post-membrane) PO2 500 mmHg, SO2 100%. Despite this, systemic arterial SaO2 remains only 86%. What does the large pre- to post-oxygenator oxygen difference indicate?
options: Minimal recirculation and good oxygenator (membrane lung) function
Inadequate ECMO blood flow relative to the patient's cardiac output
Excessive native lung shunt fraction unrelated to the ECMO circuit
Significant recirculation of oxygenated blood within the ECMO circuit
Failure of the membrane oxygenator requiring circuit exchange
questions.explanation: A large PO2/SO2 rise across the oxygenator shows the membrane lung is oxygenating blood efficiently and that recirculation (oxygenated return blood being immediately re-drained) is minimal — recirculation would instead narrow this pre/post difference by raising the pre-oxygenator saturation. The persistent low systemic SaO2 despite this reflects admixture of ECMO-oxygenated blood with poorly oxygenated native pulmonary blood flow, not a circuit problem.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man has an in-hospital cardiac arrest in ventricular fibrillation. He has now received five shocks in total, with adrenaline first given after the third. Between shocks the rhythm has converted briefly to organised complexes without a pulse before fibrillating again. Which amiodarone regimen is correct?
options: No amiodarone, since the rhythm has converted between shocks on several occasions
150 mg after the third shock and a further 300 mg after the fifth shock is given
300 mg only when the fibrillation is refractory rather than recurrent in nature
A total of 300 mg after the third shock and a further 150 mg after the fifth
300 mg after the third shock only, with no further dose thereafter
questions.explanation: European guidance gives 300 mg of amiodarone after three shocks and a further 150 mg after five, and the 2025 revision states explicitly that this applies whether the shockable rhythm is sequential and refractory or intermittent and recurrent. The distinction between refractory and recurrent fibrillation is the trap, because it was previously used to justify withholding the second dose. Lidocaine 100 mg with a further 50 mg after five shocks is the alternative where amiodarone is unavailable or local policy differs.

questions.question: Regarding monitoring and quality of cardiopulmonary resuscitation, evaluate each statement.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The rhythm assessment should be completed within five seconds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Waveform capnography is used to monitor the quality of chest compressions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Point-of-care ultrasound should be performed at every rhythm check whatever the delay it causes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sudden rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide may indicate return of spontaneous circulation.

questions.explanation: Capnography serves three purposes during resuscitation: confirming tracheal tube position, giving continuous feedback on compression quality, and signalling return of circulation through an abrupt rise. The 2025 revision halved the permitted rhythm check from ten seconds to five and asks that any shock be delivered within five seconds, reflecting how strongly outcome depends on minimising pauses. Focused ultrasound is valuable for identifying reversible causes but must be performed by someone competent enough not to prolong the pause, so it is not mandated at every check.

questions.question: A 71-year-old woman collapses four days after hip arthroplasty and is found in pulseless electrical activity. During a rhythm check, focused echocardiography shows a dilated, poorly contracting right ventricle with a small underfilled left ventricle. What is the most appropriate specific intervention?
options: Give calcium chloride with sodium bicarbonate empirically during the arrest
Stop resuscitation after twenty minutes, since the outcome here is hopeless
Perform immediate pericardiocentesis for presumed cardiac tamponade instead
Give a thrombolytic drug and continue resuscitation for 60 to 90 minutes
Give a fluid bolus of 30 mL/kg and otherwise continue standard resuscitation
questions.explanation: The combination of recent major orthopaedic surgery, pulseless electrical activity and an acutely dilated right ventricle points to pulmonary embolism, and European guidance recommends considering immediate thrombolysis when embolism is the suspected or confirmed cause. The essential corollary is that resuscitation must then continue for a further 60 to 90 minutes to allow the drug to work, so stopping at the usual point discards the only intervention that could help. Aggressive fluid loading is the most harmful wrong answer here because it worsens an already overloaded right ventricle.

questions.question: The World Health Organization defines palliative care as an approach that improves quality of life of patients and families facing life-threatening illness. Which element is EXPLICITLY included in this definition?
options: Palliative care focuses exclusively on physical symptom management during the final days of life
Palliative care and intensive care are mutually exclusive and cannot be delivered simultaneously
Palliative care begins only after all curative treatments have been exhausted and the patient is actively dying — it is incompatible with concurrent intensive care interventions
Prevention and relief of suffering through early identification, assessment, and treatment of pain and other physical, psychological, social, and spiritual problems
Palliative care is limited to in-patient hospice settings and does not apply to ICU environments
questions.explanation: The WHO definition of palliative care explicitly encompasses: prevention and relief of suffering through early identification, impeccable assessment, and treatment of pain and other physical, psychological, social, and spiritual problems. It applies to patients and families facing life-threatening illness — not only those at the very end of life. Palliative care is therefore complementary to, not exclusive of, intensive care. Integration has been associated with shorter ICU stay without increased mortality, improved patient quality of life, and greater family satisfaction.

questions.question: The WHO SAVE LIVES Clean Your Hands initiative identifies 5 specific moments at which hand hygiene must be performed. Which of the following is NOT one of the 5 WHO-designated moments?
options: After removing personal protective equipment (PPE) following patient contact
After touching a patient
After body fluid exposure or risk
After touching patient surroundings, near the end of a period of direct patient care
Before touching a patient
questions.explanation: The 5 WHO SAVE LIVES moments are: (1) before touching a patient, (2) before clean/aseptic procedures, (3) after body fluid exposure/risk, (4) after touching a patient, (5) after touching patient surroundings. 'After removing PPE' is a common and sensible practice but is NOT one of the 5 official WHO moments. This is a plausible distractor because PPE removal is taught alongside hand hygiene in infection control training, but the WHO moments framework does not include it explicitly.

questions.question: Regarding the practical management of withdrawing life-sustaining treatment (LST) in ICU:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Withholding and withdrawing LST are considered morally and legally equivalent in most countries, though many clinicians subjectively find withholding easier

statements.label: B
statements.text: When withdrawing LST, vasopressors and antibiotics should be tapered gradually over 24–48 hours to avoid physiological instability

statements.label: C
statements.text: There is no objective maximum dose for analgesics or sedatives used to achieve adequate symptom control at the end of life

statements.label: D
statements.text: Nutritional support must always be continued during end-of-life care to prevent patient distress from starvation

questions.explanation: When withdrawing LST, medications not serving the comfort-care goal should be discontinued without tapering — tapering vasopressors or antibiotics is not required. Analgesics and sedatives should be titrated upwards to achieve symptom control, with no prescribed ceiling dose. Withholding and withdrawing are ethically equivalent, though clinician discomfort with withdrawing is well-documented. Regarding nutrition: at end of life, nutrition may be discontinued as there is no medical need for caloric intake; fluids should be provided only as required for symptom control, in accordance with any applicable legal requirements.

questions.question: Does new bundle branch block complicating acute anterior myocardial infarction carry prognostic significance?
options: Yes, but only because it delays diagnosis of the infarct
No, bundle branch block is a benign finding in this context
Yes, it is associated with increased risk of early death from pump failure and ventricular tachyarrhythmias
No, prognosis is unaffected once reperfusion is achieved
Yes, but exclusively due to increased bleeding risk with anticoagulation
questions.explanation: New BBB complicating anterior MI carries a poor prognosis, with early death occurring from pump failure and ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, reflecting the large territory of myocardium at risk. It is not simply a diagnostic delay or a benign finding.

questions.question: Following cardioversion of a wide complex tachycardia, an echocardiogram shows a dilated, diffusely hypo- to akinetic left ventricle (ejection fraction 20-25%) with moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation (see figure). Coronary angiography shows no significant coronary artery disease. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
Ischaemic cardiomyopathy
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy
Non-ischaemic (idiopathic) dilated cardiomyopathy
questions.explanation: A dilated, globally hypokinetic left ventricle with significant mitral regurgitation and no significant coronary artery disease on angiography points to a non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy; the specific aetiology often remains unidentified despite investigation, as in this case. Ischaemic cardiomyopathy is excluded by the normal angiogram, and the findings are not typical of Takotsubo, hypertrophic, or predominantly right ventricular disease.

questions.question: A 59-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency room with acute onset of severe headache, nausea, and vomiting. Her blood pressure is 180/90 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals bibasilar rales and no focal neurologic signs. The cardiac troponin I is elevated at 0.65 ng/dL (normal: <0.10 ng/dL). Computed tomography (CT) of the brain demonstrates an acute intracerebral haemorrhage. Which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?
options: ECG changes and elevated cTnT levels are more commonly seen in association with subarachnoid haemorrhage
A ruptured coronary plaque with partially occlusive thrombus is likely present
Beta blockers may be effective at controlling ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation in this situation
The cardiac abnormalities in the setting of acute brain injury can be attributed increased sympathetic nervous system activity
The magnitude of peak troponin elevation in such a patient correlates with a poor cardiovascular outcome
questions.explanation: The false statement is that a ruptured coronary plaque with partially occlusive thrombus is likely present — this is NOT likely in this context. Brain-heart syndrome causes cardiac abnormalities via autonomic dysfunction (sympathetic surge) and excessive myocardial catecholamine release — WITHOUT primary coronary plaque rupture or thrombus formation. ECG changes/elevated troponin are MORE COMMON with subarachnoid haemorrhage than intracerebral haemorrhage. The magnitude of peak troponin DOES predict adverse cardiac outcome. Beta blockers are useful for arrhythmia control.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department because of severe chest pain after cocaine use. His medical history is notable for several years of intermittent cocaine use and cigarette smoking. He has no other known cardiac risk factors.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Mechanisms of cocaine-related myocardial ischemia and infarction include coronary arterial vasoconstriction and enhanced platelet aggregation

statements.label: B
statements.text: Cocaine use increases the risk of myocardial infarction (MI) 24-fold in individuals otherwise at low risk for MI

statements.label: C
statements.text: The risk of MI after cocaine is related to the amount ingested and the frequency of its use

statements.label: D
statements.text: Left ventricular systolic dysfunction can occur both acutely and after long-term cocaine use

questions.explanation: Cocaine MI risk is NOT related to amount ingested or frequency — this is a critical distinction. LV dysfunction occurs acutely (metabolic disturbances) and chronically (cardiomyopathy from repeated sympathetic stimulation). Mechanisms include coronary vasoconstriction, enhanced platelet aggregation, and thrombogenicity. Cocaine increases MI risk 25-fold (not 24-fold) over the 60 minutes following use in individuals otherwise at low risk.

questions.question: The Na+/K+ pump is:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Inhibited by digitalis.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Decreases intracellular action potential.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Exchanges 3 potassium ions for 2 sodium ions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: ATPase dependent.

questions.explanation: The Na+/K+ pump is ATPase-dependent and inhibited by digitalis glycosides. It exchanges three sodium ions out for two potassium ions in (not the reverse) — an electrogenic exchange that increases the intracellular negative (resting) potential, promoting repolarisation and maintaining low intracellular Na+ and high intracellular K+; this is not accurately described as 'decreasing the action potential'.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man ventilated for six days develops new purulent secretions, a rising oxygen requirement and a new radiographic infiltrate. He is hypotensive and has just been started on noradrenaline. Bronchoalveolar lavage has been sent for quantitative culture. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Start empirical antibiotics now and use a lavage threshold of 10⁴ CFU/mL to de-escalate
Treat on tracheal aspirate Gram stain alone and avoid bronchoalveolar lavage entirely
Withhold antibiotics until the quantitative culture result becomes available in 48 hours
Start antibiotics only if the lavage grows more than 10⁶ CFU/mL of a pathogen
Start antibiotics and continue the same regimen regardless of the culture result
questions.explanation: In a patient with septic shock, empirical therapy must not wait for microbiology, while the quantitative lavage threshold of 10 000 colony-forming units per millilitre then guides whether treatment is narrowed or stopped. Withholding antibiotics pending culture is the answer that looks like good stewardship but costs lives in shock, and a threshold of 10⁶ applies to endotracheal aspirates rather than lavage. Committing to a fixed regimen regardless of results abandons de-escalation, which is the main purpose of obtaining a quantitative sample at all.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man with suspected pneumococcal meningitis had blood cultures taken and received ceftriaxone in the emergency department 40 minutes ago. Lumbar puncture has just been performed and shows turbid fluid with Gram-positive diplococci. Dexamethasone has not yet been given. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give dexamethasone only if he deteriorates neurologically over the coming hours
Withhold dexamethasone because the first antibiotic dose has been given
Give dexamethasone now and continue it four times daily for the next four days
Give one dose of dexamethasone and stop once the pathogen is confirmed
Withhold dexamethasone and give mannitol for presumed cerebral oedema
questions.explanation: Adjunctive dexamethasone works best when it precedes or accompanies the first antibiotic dose, but European guidance still supports starting it within a few hours afterwards rather than abandoning it altogether. The standard course is 10 mg every six hours for four days, so stopping after a single dose forfeits most of the benefit on mortality and hearing loss. Mannitol treats raised intracranial pressure and has no role as a substitute for the anti-inflammatory effect that dexamethasone provides in the subarachnoid space.

questions.question: Regarding the scoring system in sepsis, which of the following is correct?
options: Organ dysfunction as assessed by the SOFA score is an important criterion for the diagnosis of Sepsis
qSOFA score is a well-validated tool for suspicion of sepsis in ICU
qSOFA score essentially rules out Sepsis
qSOFA is essential criteria for diagnosis of Sepsis
qSOFA score requires laboratory values
questions.explanation: Organ dysfunction assessed by SOFA score is a key criterion for sepsis diagnosis (Sepsis-3). qSOFA includes three clinical criteria with no laboratory values (SBP ≤100, RR ≥22, altered mental status). qSOFA ≥2 has been validated as a screening tool outside ICU (ER, wards) but NOT in the ICU. A qSOFA of 1 does not rule out sepsis. Recent evidence has also challenged qSOFA's utility even outside the ICU.

questions.question: Regarding initial fluid resuscitation in sepsis:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Central venous pressure and central venous oxygen saturation are the parameters of choice

statements.label: B
statements.text: Fluid resuscitation should be initiated immediately

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dynamic measures to guide fluid resuscitation are recommended over clinical examination

statements.label: D
statements.text: At least 30 mL/kg should be administered within the first 24 hours

questions.explanation: Fluid resuscitation should be initiated immediately in sepsis-induced tissue hypoperfusion. The SSC recommends at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid within the first 3 hours (not 24 hours). Dynamic measures are recommended over physical examination or static parameters alone. CVP and ScvO2 are NOT the parameters of choice — dynamic measures (PLR, PPV, IVC variation, EEOM) are preferred; static parameters like CVP poorly predict fluid responsiveness.

questions.question: Regarding adjunctive dexamethasone in community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults, evaluate each statement.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It is contraindicated when the patient presents with septic shock.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It should be discontinued once a pathogen other than pneumococcus or Haemophilus influenzae is identified.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It reduces the incidence of hearing loss.

questions.explanation: The mortality benefit of dexamethasone in high-income settings is driven almost entirely by pneumococcal disease, and the hearing benefit is well demonstrated across pathogens, which is why it is started empirically before the organism is known. Once a different pathogen is confirmed the rationale disappears and the steroid is stopped. Septic shock is not a contraindication; corticosteroids are given in that setting for a separate haemodynamic indication, so withholding dexamethasone on those grounds confuses two different treatment rationales.

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation presents three hours after symptom onset with a 20 mL lobar haemorrhage and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13. Her last dose was eight hours ago. Which haemostatic strategy is most appropriate?
options: Andexanet alfa, accepting an increased risk of thrombotic events
Tranexamic acid combined with prothrombin complex concentrate
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, which has proven superiority for haemostasis
Idarucizumab given as two consecutive 2.5 g intravenous boluses
Fresh frozen plasma with vitamin K and repeat imaging at six hours
questions.explanation: Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for direct factor Xa inhibitors and achieved superior haemostatic efficacy compared with usual care, predominantly prothrombin complex concentrate, in a randomised trial of acute intracranial haemorrhage. The trade-off must be stated: thrombotic events were more frequent and neither mortality nor functional outcome improved, so guidelines differ in how strongly they recommend it and prothrombin complex concentrate remains a reasonable option where andexanet is unavailable. Idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran, and plasma with vitamin K reverses vitamin K antagonists far too slowly for an expanding haematoma.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage secured by coiling twelve hours ago is admitted to the neurointensive care unit. He is haemodynamically stable and has a functioning enteral feeding tube. Regarding nimodipine, which management is most appropriate?
options: Enteral nimodipine started only if transcranial Doppler velocities rise
Intravenous nimodipine infusion titrated against mean arterial pressure
Enteral nimodipine 60 mg every four hours started immediately
Intrathecal nimodipine via an external ventricular drain as first line
No nimodipine, since the ruptured aneurysm has already been secured
questions.explanation: Oral or enteral nimodipine is the only pharmacological intervention with high-quality evidence of improved functional outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, and it should begin as soon as the diagnosis is made rather than waiting for signs of vasospasm. The intravenous formulation is the most plausible wrong answer in a sedated intensive care patient, but it causes more hypotension and has not shown the same outcome benefit in pooled analyses. Securing the aneurysm removes the rebleeding risk but does nothing about delayed cerebral ischaemia, which is what nimodipine addresses.

questions.question: Which of the following clinical presentations is most typical in ischaemic stroke in the region supplied by the middle cerebral artery?
options: Ipsilateral sensory deficit of face and arm more than leg
Contralateral motor deficit of face and arm/leg (arm more than leg)
Bilateral sensory deficits in the face
Contralateral motoric deficit of face and arm/leg (leg more than arm)
Ataxic hemiparesis
questions.explanation: Face and arm weakness are more prominent in MCA stroke due to the middle cerebral artery supply to the lateral aspect of the primary motor cortex. Remember the homunculus! A leg-predominant deficit suggests ACA territory instead. Ataxic hemiparesis is a lacunar/posterior fossa syndrome, not an MCA pattern. The correct answer is: Contralateral motor deficit of face and arm/leg (arm more than leg).

questions.question: Regarding the definitions and staging of status epilepticus, evaluate each statement.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Super-refractory status epilepticus is defined by recurrence within twelve hours of starting anaesthesia.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Convulsive status epilepticus is defined by seizure activity lasting 30 minutes or longer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Refractory status epilepticus is defined by failure of two adequately dosed antiseizure medications of different classes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Non-convulsive status epilepticus can be diagnosed reliably on clinical grounds without electroencephalography.

questions.explanation: The operational threshold was shortened to five minutes of continuous convulsive activity, or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness, precisely because waiting half an hour allows the pharmacoresistance that follows receptor trafficking to develop. Refractory disease means failure of a benzodiazepine plus one further adequately dosed agent from a different class, and super-refractory means persistence or recurrence despite more than 24 hours of anaesthesia. Non-convulsive status has no reliable clinical signature and is the reason electroencephalography is required in any patient who fails to wake after a convulsive episode.

questions.question: In a patient with an exacerbation of COPD or asthma, warning signs of impending respiratory arrest include the following, EXCEPT:
options: Tachycardia (110/min)
Presence of pulsus paradoxus
Silent chest
Lethargy
questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] ESICM showed no facit and no feedback text for this question after an incorrect answer. Best clinical reasoning: severe hypoxaemia, lethargy, a silent chest, and pulsus paradoxus are all classic markers of life-threatening/near-fatal asthma or COPD. A heart rate of 110/min is only modest tachycardia (often simply reflecting beta-agonist treatment) and is not itself a marker of impending arrest - marked bradycardia or a falling heart rate would be more concerning. Verify against the original ESICM material if possible.

questions.question: A 62 year-old man with past medical history of severe COPD is transferred from the emergency department to the ICU suffering from severe respiratory distress and clinical and radiographic evidence of left-sided pneumonia. He has a temperature of 39.1°C, respiratory rate of 34 breaths/min and SpO2 75% with supplementary oxygen 8 l/min by a face mask. His heart rate is 125 beats/min, and the blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. Regarding the management of this patient: Which of the following is correct?
options: The use of electric impedance tomography has been shown to reduce VILI and mortality in ARDS
Pneumothorax cannot be diagnosed by ultrasound
An increase in end-expiratory lung volume after increase of PEEP as measured by nitrogen washin/washout methods clearly indicates lung recruitment
Nitrogen washin/washout methods will overestimate end-expiratory lung volumes in this patient
Chest x-ray can be used in order to diagnose ARDS
questions.explanation: Bilateral opacities on chest X-ray are part of the Berlin ARDS diagnostic criteria, so chest X-ray can indeed be used to help diagnose ARDS. Gas dilution (nitrogen washin/washout) methods measure lung gas volume but cannot distinguish whether an increase is due to recruitment of collapsed units or distention of already-open units, so an increase in end-expiratory lung volume after raising PEEP is not 'clearly' diagnostic of recruitment. Electric impedance tomography has not been shown to reduce mortality. Pneumothorax CAN be diagnosed by ultrasound — absent lung sliding, absent B-lines, lung point. This patient has severe COPD; lung regions with long time constants are measured poorly by gas dilution methods, causing underestimation rather than overestimation of lung volume.

questions.question: In making the triage decision as to whether a patient with an acute exacerbation of COPD or asthma needs ventilatory support initiated quickly, important signs include the following, EXCEPT:
options: Inadequate response to initial therapy
Haemodynamic instability
Worsening of respiratory acidosis (pH <7.25)
Worsening of hypoxaemia (PaO2 <5.3 kPa)
PaCO2 >10 kPa
questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] ESICM showed no facit and no feedback text for this question after an incorrect answer. Best clinical reasoning: an isolated PaCO2 threshold is not itself a validated trigger for urgent ventilatory support, since some patients (particularly chronic CO2 retainers) tolerate a chronically elevated PaCO2 - it is the accompanying pH/acidosis, altered mental status, hypoxaemia and haemodynamic instability that indicate urgency, consistent with the rest of this module. Verify against the original ESICM material if possible.

questions.question: In a patient with severe ARDS being placed prone, what is the aim of proning? Are the following statements true or false?

statements.label: A
statements.text: Buying time for lung healing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Improving oxygenation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Unloading the left cardiac ventricle.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Preventing ventilator-induced lung injury.

questions.explanation: Oxygenation improves in roughly 50–75% of patients placed prone (statement 1 true). Proning homogenises the distribution of lung stress and strain, which is thought to reduce ventilator-induced lung injury (statement 3 true) — this is the main physiological rationale, not simply 'buying time' (statement 4 false). Proning unloads the right ventricle, not the left ventricle (statement 2 false).

questions.question: A 55-year-old man was admitted to the ICU with hypotension related to acute cholecystitis and a gram-negative bacteraemia. He had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension and a raised body mass index. Baseline estimated GFR is 45ml/min/1.73m2 and urinary albumin to creatinine ratio 15.3ml/mmol. He developed ARDS requiring invasive mechanical ventilation and oliguric renal failure requiring RRT. He is commenced on CRRT. High intensity renal replacement therapy in this scenario is associated with:
options: Increased levels of niacin which promotes tubular regeneration
Increased risk of dialysis disequilibrium
Longer period of time on dialysis at 28 days
Faster recovery of his renal function
Improved membrane biocompatibility from increased blood flow
questions.explanation: High-intensity RRT is associated with a longer period of time on dialysis at 28 days, as shown in meta-analyses of studies examining outcomes following higher renal replacement intensity. Faster renal recovery has not been noted. High-intensity RRT causes decreased — not increased — levels of niacin (a precursor for nicotinamide dinucleotide required for tubular regeneration). Dialysis disequilibrium is unlikely during CRRT, which removes solutes slowly and continuously.

questions.question: A 72 y.o. woman is admitted to the ICU with community-acquired pneumonia and AKI Stage 2. She appears euvolemic after initial resuscitation. The treating team considers a furosemide stress test to guide further management. Which of the following best describes the correct administration and interpretation of this test?
options: Administer 0.5 mg/kg IV furosemide; urine output <100 mL in 2 hours predicts progression
Administer 1.0 mg/kg IV furosemide (or 1.5 mg/kg if furosemide-naïve); urine output <200 mL in 2 hours predicts high risk of Stage 3 AKI and RRT need
Administer 1.0 mg/kg IV furosemide; the test is valid only in Stage 1 AKI, not Stage 2
Administer 1.0 mg/kg IV furosemide; urine output <200 mL in 2 hours is specific for glomerular injury, not tubular
The furosemide stress test should only be performed after urinary biomarkers (NGAL, TIMP-2 × IGFBP-7) return negative, as it is inferior to biomarkers
questions.explanation: The furosemide stress test uses 1.0 mg/kg IV (or 1.5 mg/kg in furosemide-naïve patients). Urine output <200 mL in 2 hours predicts progression to Stage 3 AKI and need for RRT with high sensitivity and specificity. It assesses tubular function — the ability to respond to furosemide requires intact tubular secretory mechanisms. The test is validated in Stage 1–2 AKI, not restricted to Stage 1 alone. It assesses tubular, not glomerular, function. It is complementary to biomarkers, not subordinate to them.

questions.question: Certain co-morbidities are associated with an increased risk of developing AKI in hospital. These include:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Hypertension

statements.label: B
statements.text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

statements.label: C
statements.text: Obesity

statements.label: D
statements.text: Heart failure

questions.explanation: 20% of patients admitted to hospital with heart failure will develop an AKI and the development of AKI is associated with an increased risk of mortality. COPD is an independent risk factor for the development of both CKD and AKI. Obesity may increase the risk of AKI through changes to venous blood flow and pressures and through systemic inflammation. Hypertension is an independent risk factor for AKI.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man with NAFLD-cirrhosis and ascites is orientated in time and place but has a shortened attention span with impaired performance of simple mental tasks. Based on the West Haven Criteria, what grade of hepatic encephalopathy does this represent?
options: Grade 3
Grade 2
Grade 1
Grade 0
Grade 4
questions.explanation: West Haven grade 1 is characterised by trivial lack of awareness, euphoria or anxiety, a shortened attention span, and impaired performance of simple mental tasks such as addition/subtraction — matching this patient's orientation to time/place but reduced attention span. Grade 0 would show no detectable change; grade 2 adds disorientation and personality change.

questions.question: A 27-year-old male presents with agitation, hypotension, hypoglycaemia and severe lactic acidosis of unclear cause, with a tender epigastrium and recent travel to South East Asia. Beyond routine haematology/biochemistry, which additional panel of tests should be requested?
options: Serum tumour markers (AFP, CA19-9)
Coagulation profile, arterial ammonia, viral hepatitis serology (A/B/C/E) and HIV, blood cultures, and toxicology screen
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis via lumbar puncture
Serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urinary copper only
Autoimmune liver screen (ANA, ASMA) only
questions.explanation: A patient with acute confusion, deranged liver enzymes and suspected acute liver failure needs a broad first-line panel: coagulation, renal/hepatic function, arterial ammonia (encephalopathy), viral hepatitis serology and HIV, blood cultures, and a toxicology screen (including paracetamol level) — narrower panels (copper studies, autoimmune screen alone) or CSF analysis are not first-line here.

questions.question: Regarding aetiology-specific therapies for acute liver failure:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Activated charcoal and high-dose intravenous penicillin have proven survival benefit in mushroom poisoning-related liver failure

statements.label: B
statements.text: Lamivudine or entecavir may be used for acute hepatitis B-related liver failure

statements.label: C
statements.text: N-acetylcysteine is recommended for acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure

statements.label: D
statements.text: Corticosteroids are first-line therapy for Wilson disease-associated acute liver failure

questions.explanation: Aetiology-specific therapy is available for only a few causes of ALF: N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen toxicity, and antivirals such as lamivudine/entecavir for hepatitis B. Corticosteroids are reserved for autoimmune hepatitis, not Wilson disease (which is treated with chelation/plasmapheresis). Activated charcoal and high-dose IV penicillin for mushroom poisoning remain of unproven benefit despite their use.

questions.question: A 41 year old female is admitted to the ICU with a 30% TBSA (20% full thickness, 10% partial thickness) burn injury earlier in the day. Fluid resuscitation has been commenced by the Emergency Department prior to ICU admission. She is intubated and ventilated with FiO2 0.4. Her HR is 110bpm with MAP 72 unsupported. On examination she is warm and well perfused with capillary refill time of <2 seconds. She has recently had a urinary catheter sited which has drained 200mls of residual volume. How will you approach ongoing fluid resuscitation?
options: Urine output should be closely monitored, and fluid rate increased if it falls below 1ml/kg ideal body weight
Colloids such as human albumin solution should be administered for fluid boluses as required
The total body surface area of only full thickness burn should be used to calculate the initial fluid resuscitation volume using the Parkland formula
Balanced crystalloid solution should be used for fluid resuscitation guided by hourly urine output
After calculating the total volume to be administered via the Parkland formula, the patient should receive half of the total volume in the first 8 hours after hospitalisation
questions.explanation: Balanced crystalloid guided by hourly urine output (target 0.5-1 ml/kg IBW/hour) is the standard approach; colloids are reserved once volumes significantly exceed the anticipated requirement. The first half of the Parkland-calculated volume is given over the first 8 hours from the time of burn injury, not from hospitalisation, making A a near-miss. Total (not only full-thickness) TBSA is used in the formula, and the target urine output threshold is 0.5-1 ml/kg, not simply 'below 1ml/kg' as a trigger to increase the rate.

questions.question: An 84-year-old nursing home resident is admitted with a sodium of 168 mmol/L that has developed gradually over several days. She is drowsy but haemodynamically stable with a free water deficit estimated at four litres. What correction target is most appropriate?
options: Lower the sodium by 1 mmol/L per hour until it reaches 150 mmol/L
Lower the sodium below 145 mmol/L within six hours
Replace the entire calculated deficit over the first eight hours only
Withhold free water until the neurological state has improved fully
Lower the sodium by no more than about 10 mmol/L over 24 hours
questions.explanation: Chronic hypernatraemia allows the brain to accumulate organic osmoles, and lowering the sodium faster than roughly 10 mmol/L per day risks cerebral oedema and seizures as water moves back into cells. Ongoing losses must be added to the calculated deficit, which is why the correction is guided by repeated measurement rather than by a single formula. Rapid correction is appropriate only in acute hypernatraemia developing over hours, where the osmolar adaptation has not had time to occur.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man is found unconscious at home and brought to the Emergency Department. He was started on oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreathing mask; SpO2 was 90%, blood pressure 110/65 mmHg, heart rate 120/min, respiratory rate 40/min, temperature 36°C, breathing deep and laboured. Pupils were 4 mm, equal and reactive. He moaned to pain and flexed both upper extremities but did not open his eyes. He has a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine and has been drinking excess alcohol for about a year, since his wife died. He lives alone; family last spoke to him by phone the previous night around 10 PM and he sounded fine. No empty pill bottles were found, but there were 3 empty beer bottles nearby. An arterial blood gas just before intubation showed: pH 7.05, pCO2 30 mmHg, pO2 65 mmHg, HCO3- 10 mEq/L. You decide to intubate the patient. When intubating this patient extra caution is required because:

statements.label: A
statements.text: There is increased risk for hypotension

statements.label: B
statements.text: There is tachycardia

statements.label: C
statements.text: There is severe acidosis

statements.label: D
statements.text: The time of last meal is not known

questions.explanation: This patient has a severe, decompensated metabolic acidosis (pH 7.05, HCO3- 10) with respiratory compensation (tachypnoea, low pCO2). Induction agents and positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate hypotension and cardiovascular collapse in severely acidotic patients, and any drop in minute ventilation during intubation removes the respiratory compensation, worsening the acidaemia. His unknown last-meal time raises aspiration risk, and his tachycardia reflects physiological compensation that can be blunted by induction agents — all of these make airway management higher-risk and warrant extra caution and preparation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding antibiotic pharmacokinetics is INCORRECT?
options: In simple PK models, volume of distribution (Vd) is a constant that relates the dose administered to the plasma concentration at time zero
The time constant corresponds to a reduction in concentration to 37% of the original value
Tetracycline bioavailability is reduced by milk intake
A large elimination rate constant (k) produces a short elimination half-life (t1/2)
Drugs absorbed from the buccal mucosa are subject to first-pass metabolism
questions.explanation: Unlike gastrointestinal absorption, buccal (and rectal) mucosal absorption drains directly into the systemic circulation and bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism, which makes the claim that buccal absorption undergoes first-pass metabolism the incorrect one. The remaining statements are accurate: Vd = dose/C0 in simple models; the time constant is the time for concentration to fall to 37% of its previous value (with about 95% of a process complete after 3 time-constants); half-life is inversely related to the elimination rate constant (t1/2 = 0.693/k); and calcium in milk chelates tetracycline, reducing its bioavailability. (Peck, Hill & Williams, Pharmacology for Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, 3rd ed., 2008)

questions.question: Which of the following factors does not affect drug clearance in patients with acute kidney injury (AKI)?
options: Change in protein binding
Type of renal replacement therapy
Endogenous kidney function
Mode of action of the drug
Hypoalbuminemia
questions.explanation: A drug's mode of action does not determine how it is cleared. Hypoalbuminaemia and altered protein binding change the volume of distribution, and the renal replacement modality and any residual kidney function all affect clearance.

questions.question: How is the clearance in continuous veno-venous hemodialysis (CVVHD) calculated?
options: Blood flow rate (Qb) divided by Dialysate flow rate (Qd) multiplied by saturation coefficient (SA)
Dialysate flow rate (Qd) multiplied by sieving coefficient (SC)
(Qeff + Qd) multiplied by saturation coefficient (SA)
Dialysate flow rate (Qd) multiplied by saturation coefficient (SA)
Effluent flow rate (Qeff) multiplied by sieving coefficient (SC)
questions.explanation: For CVVHD, drug clearance is estimated as dialysate flow rate multiplied by the saturation coefficient. Hemofiltration uses effluent flow times the sieving coefficient and hemodiafiltration sums both flows, so the other formulae describe different modalities.

questions.question: In the setting of intermittent forms of renal replacement therapy (RRT), which administration strategy is typically recommended for time-dependent antibiotics?
options: Loading dose before the RRT session and top-up dose after the session
Continuous infusion during the RRT session
Administration before the RRT session
Intermittent infusion during the RRT session
Administration after the RRT session
questions.explanation: For time-dependent antibiotics on intermittent RRT, giving the dose after the session preserves therapeutic concentrations, since dosing during dialysis risks removal and sub-therapeutic levels. Concentration-dependent agents may instead be given before the session so peaks can be cleared to limit toxicity.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man is admitted to the ICU after presenting a week earlier with flu-like symptoms. He is diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia; CT chest shows a diffuse ground-glass appearance of the lung parenchyma with bilateral cavitations. Empirical therapy for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is started while sputum and blood culture results are awaited. How should antibiotic treatment be guided in this patient?
options: Empirical MRSA coverage should continue even if cultures come back negative
Linezolid is preferred over vancomycin due to a lower mortality rate
In patients with good renal function, vancomycin once daily is the optimal pharmacokinetic profile
If the MIC for vancomycin is >2 mcg/mL, daptomycin should be used
The target vancomycin trough concentration is 15-20 mcg/mL
questions.explanation: Vancomycin penetrates lung tissue poorly, and the exposure parameter that best predicts efficacy is AUC:MIC - an AUC:MIC >400 is associated with improved clinical and microbiological cure for staphylococcal pneumonia, which corresponds to a trough target of 15-20 mcg/mL. Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and must not be used for pneumonia regardless of vancomycin MIC. Linezolid and vancomycin have shown comparable cure rates for community-acquired MRSA pneumonia (linezolid has a specific advantage in nosocomial pneumonia per the Zephyr study). There is no recommendation to continue empirical MRSA cover once cultures return negative and the organism is not isolated. With preserved renal function, 12-hourly dosing - not once daily - is generally the optimal PK/PD profile, though some evidence supports 2 g once daily as satisfactory. (Chastre et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2014;20(Suppl 4):19-36; Carballo et al., Farm Hosp 2017;41(2):187-203)

questions.question: Regarding pharmacodynamics (PD) of antibiotics:

statements.label: A
statements.text: The MIC provides no information regarding the time course of the antimicrobial effect

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adjusting antibiotic dosage to a PK/PD target has been reported to improve clinical and microbiologic outcomes

statements.label: C
statements.text: PD targets have been extensively studied in a considerable number of clinical studies

statements.label: D
statements.text: For beta-lactams, increasing drug concentrations has major effects on the extent of bacterial killing

questions.explanation: Beta-lactams are concentration-independent ("time-dependent") killers, so raising the concentration further does little to increase the extent of killing once it is above the MIC - what matters is the time spent above MIC. The MIC itself is a static endpoint from a fixed incubation period and says nothing about the rate or time-course of killing. Clinical outcome data linking PK/PD targets to outcomes are comparatively sparse, but the studies that exist do suggest benefit from dosing adjusted to PK/PD targets.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding renal replacement therapies (RRT) in the ICU are true?

statements.label: A
statements.text: RRT techniques primarily focus on compensating for processes of secretion and metabolism

statements.label: B
statements.text: Intermittent haemodialysis (IHD) relies on convection for solute removal

statements.label: C
statements.text: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is administered over short periods, typically 4-6 hours

statements.label: D
statements.text: The prescribed clearance for CRRT is often overestimated compared to the actual delivered clearance

questions.explanation: Renal replacement primarily compensates for clearance and excretion, not secretion and metabolism, so that statement is false. Intermittent haemodialysis relies on diffusion rather than convection, and continuous therapy runs over roughly 24 hours rather than a few hours; only the point that prescribed CRRT clearance often exceeds the delivered clearance is true.

questions.question: Regarding colistin:

statements.label: A
statements.text: It is not absorbed through the oral mucosa or gastrointestinal tract

statements.label: B
statements.text: It has questionable clinical efficacy when inhaled and should therefore not be used

statements.label: C
statements.text: It has been reported to have very high protein binding

statements.label: D
statements.text: It has no post-antibiotic effect (PAE)

questions.explanation: Colistin (sulfate) is not usefully absorbed from the GI tract, which is why oral/enteral colistin is used only for bowel decontamination rather than systemic infection - parenteral treatment instead requires colistin methanesulfonate (CMS). Reported protein binding is around 59-90%. Colistin shows a modest post-antibiotic effect at high concentrations against P. aeruginosa, and killing correlates best with fAUC/MIC. Despite poor lung distribution, published data support adding CMS aerosol delivery to IV therapy for pulmonary infections in critically ill patients, so inhalation is not without a role. (Falagas, Kasiakou & Saravolatz, Clin Infect Dis 2005;40(9):1333-1341)

questions.question: A patient with severe ARDS on veno-venous ECMO (femoral-jugular cannulation) has persistent SaO2 86% despite a well-functioning ECMO circuit and minimal recirculation. Native lung compliance is very poor and the patient is already on an ultra-protective ventilation strategy. Which is the most appropriate next step to improve systemic oxygenation?
options: Decrease ECMO sweep gas flow
Increase ECMO blood (pump) flow to increase the fraction of cardiac output passing through the oxygenator
Increase mechanical ventilator FiO2 and inspiratory pressures to raise native lung contribution
Increase PEEP to maximal tolerated levels regardless of plateau pressure
Convert to veno-arterial ECMO configuration
questions.explanation: With poor native lung compliance, raising ventilator pressures risks further ventilator-induced lung injury for limited oxygenation gain. Increasing ECMO blood flow raises the ECMO-to-cardiac-output ratio, the dominant determinant of systemic oxygenation on VV-ECMO, allowing oxygenation to improve while a lung-protective ventilation strategy is maintained.

questions.question: In patients with ARDS on volume control ventilation, the stress index (the slope of the airway pressure-time curve during inspiration) has been suggested as a method of PEEP titration. Which of the following is correct?
options: Stress index < 1 indicates an increase in compliance during inflation, high system compliance and PEEP should be increased
Stress index < 1 indicates a decrease in compliance during inflation and VT or/and PEEP should be decreased
Stress index >1 indicates over-distention and PEEP should be increased
Stress index < 1 indicates a decrease in compliance during inflation and VT/and PEEP should be increased
Stress index > 1 indicates an increase in compliance during inflation and PEEP should be increased
questions.explanation: A linear increase in pressure (constant compliance, stress index = 1) suggests adequate alveolar recruitment without over-distension. If compliance IMPROVES as the lungs are inflated (progressive INCREASE in compliance, downward concavity, stress index <1), this suggests ongoing tidal recruitment and potential for additional recruitment — the recommendation is to INCREASE PEEP, which makes the statement correctly pairing stress index <1, an increase in compliance, and increasing PEEP the right answer. If compliance WORSENS as the lungs are inflated (progressive decrease in compliance, upward concavity, stress index >1), this suggests over-distension, and the recommendation is to DECREASE PEEP, VT, or both — so the statement pairing stress index >1 with increasing PEEP is wrong. The two statements describing stress index <1 as indicating a DECREASE in compliance are both wrong on that point (the opposite is true), even though one of them pairs it with the correct directional management advice to increase treatment.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct?
options: A decrease in temperature shifts Hb −O2 dissociation curve to the left (decrease Hb-O2 affinity)
A decrease in PH shifts Hb −O2 dissociation curve to the right (increase Hb-O2 affinity)
A decrease in PH shifts Hb −O2 dissociation curve to the right (decrease Hb-O2 affinity)
An increase in PH shifts Hb −O2 dissociation curve to the left (decrease Hb-O2 affinity)
An increase in temperature shifts Hb −O2 dissociation curve to the left (decrease Hb-O2 affinity)
questions.explanation: A decrease in pH (acidosis) shifts the Hb-O2 dissociation curve to the RIGHT, which DECREASES Hb-O2 affinity (Bohr effect) — the statement describing a pH decrease shifting the curve right with decreased affinity is correct as written. Increased temperature also shifts the curve right (decreased affinity), so the statement claiming it shifts left is wrong. Decreased temperature shifts the curve left (increased affinity, not decreased), so that statement is wrong too. Increased pH shifts the curve left (increased, not decreased affinity), making that statement wrong. The remaining statement describing a pH decrease shifting the curve right gets the direction right but the affinity change wrong (it claims increased rather than decreased affinity).

questions.question: Regarding recirculation inside a dialysis catheter, which of the following statement(s), is (are) TRUE?

statements.label: A
statements.text: Recirculation is low if there is a significant distance (> 2 cm) between the proximal and the distal holes of the dialysis catheter

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recirculation is increased during a RRT session if the catheter lines are "reversed" by the medical team in order to fix a "pressure" issue

statements.label: C
statements.text: The more the recirculation, the less efficient (in terms of solute clearance) the RRT session.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Recirculation is important when a 15 cm catheter is placed at the femoral site.

questions.explanation: Recirculation increases when catheter lines are reversed to fix a pressure problem, and higher recirculation reduces the solute clearance efficiency of the session. A short (15 cm) femoral catheter is prone to significant recirculation because its tip sits in a lower-flow location closer to the return line. Conversely, recirculation stays low when there is adequate separation, at least 2-3 cm, between the proximal and distal catheter holes, alongside correct tip placement in a high-flow vessel and avoidance of line reversal.

questions.question: Which of the following is/are correct?

statements.label: A
statements.text: In pressure targeted modes (PS and PCV) the pressure provided by the ventilator is independent of respiratory system mechanics (compliance and or resistance)

statements.label: B
statements.text: In pressure targeted modes (PS and PCV) the pressure provided by the ventilator depends on respiratory system mechanics (compliance and or resistance)

statements.label: C
statements.text: In volume targeted modes (VC and AVC), the inspiratory flow depends on respiratory system mechanics (compliance and or resistance)

statements.label: D
statements.text: In volume targeted modes (VCV and AVC) the pressure provided by the ventilator is independent of respiratory system mechanics (compliance and or resistance)

questions.explanation: By the equation of motion, PTOT(t) = Pmus(t) + Paw(t) = Pres(t) + Pel(t) = V'(t)×Rrs + ΔV(t)×Ers. In VOLUME-TARGETED modes (VC, AVC), the independent (pre-set) variables are flow and volume; the ventilator delivers a FIXED flow regardless of respiratory mechanics, so inspiratory flow is INDEPENDENT of compliance/resistance (C is false) and the resulting PRESSURE varies depending on mechanics (B is false, since pressure is actually DEPENDENT on mechanics in volume modes — the opposite of B's claim). In PRESSURE-TARGETED modes (PS, PCV), the independent (pre-set) variable is pressure itself; the ventilator delivers a FIXED pressure regardless of mechanics, so the pressure provided is INDEPENDENT of compliance/resistance — D is correct, and A (claiming pressure DEPENDS on mechanics in pressure modes) is false, as the resulting flow/volume — not the pressure — varies with mechanics.
